items.title: Numerical reasoning: percentages, decimals and fractions (level 2)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: At this stage the sums are still one step, but you need to move between percentages, decimals and fractions with confidence. To turn a percentage into a decimal, divide by 100: 35% is 0.35. To turn a decimal into a percentage, multiply by 100: 0.6 is 60%. A fraction becomes a percentage by dividing the top by the bottom and multiplying by 100, so 3/4 is 0.75, which is 75%. To find a fraction of an amount, divide by the bottom number and multiply by the top: 3/5 of 40 is 40 ÷ 5 = 8, then 8 × 3 = 24. To find one amount as a percentage of another, divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100: 10 out of 50 is 10 ÷ 50 = 0.2, which is 20%. For a quick percentage like 5%, find 10% and halve it. Worked example: 5% of £300. Ten per cent is £30, and half of that is £15. Be careful to read whether the question asks for the amount of a rise or the new total after the rise. A 10% rise on £24,000 is a rise of £2,400, and the new salary is £26,400. Underline what is being asked before you calculate.

questions.prompt: What is 20% of the number 150?
questions.hint: 10% of 150 is 15, so 20% is double: 30.

questions.prompt: What is 75% of the number 120?
questions.hint: 75% is three quarters: 120 ÷ 4 = 30, then 30 × 3 = 90.

questions.prompt: What is the fraction 3/5 of 40?
What percentage of 50 is 10?
The decimal 0.35 written as a percentage is which of these?
questions.hint: Multiply the decimal by 100: 0.35 × 100 = 35%.

questions.prompt: What is 5% of an amount of £300?
questions.hint: 10% is £30; half of that is £15.

questions.prompt: Which percentage is equal to the fraction 3/4?
A salary of £24,000 will rise by 10%. By how much will it rise?

items.title: Numerical reasoning: pay, prices and exchange (level 2)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Money questions at this level add a little more thinking. You may be asked for a unit price, for pay over a week or month, or for the cost of items in a different currency. The main rules are simple. To find the price of one item when you know the price of a pack, divide the price by the number of items. To find a total, multiply the price of one by how many. For weekly pay, multiply the hourly rate by the hours worked. To go from a yearly amount to a monthly amount, divide by 12. If a yearly amount needs to become weekly, divide by 52. Overtime is often paid at a higher rate, such as time and a half, which means 1.5 times the normal hourly rate. Worked example: you earn £10 an hour and work 4 hours of overtime at time and a half. The overtime rate is £10 × 1.5 = £15 an hour, so you earn £15 × 4 = £60. For currency, the question gives you a rate, such as £1 = €1.15. To change pounds into euros, multiply by the rate. Check that your answer is sensible: you should get more euros than pounds when the rate is above one.

questions.prompt: A pack of 3 notebooks costs £2.40. What is the cost of one notebook?
An employee works 35 hours a week at £11 an hour. What is her weekly pay?
A return bus ticket costs £2.30. How much does it cost to buy one for each of 5 working days?
A salary is £26,400 a year. How much is that per month?
Anwar saves £15 a week. How much will he have saved after 8 weeks?
The exchange rate is £1 = €1.15. How many euros will £40 buy?

options.text: 34.78 euros
41.15 euros
60 euros
46 euros

questions.hint: Multiply pounds by the rate: 40 × 1.15 = 46.

questions.prompt: Overtime is paid at time and a half. The normal rate is £10 an hour. How much is earned for 4 hours of overtime?
A printer cartridge went up in price from £8 to £10. How much more does it cost now?

items.title: Numerical reasoning: time, measures and dates (level 2)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Time and measure questions at this level may need a conversion with decimals or a calculation across the hour. Key conversions are worth learning: 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour, 1,000 metres in a kilometre, 1,000 grams in a kilogram and 1,000 millilitres in a litre. When you change to a smaller unit, multiply. When you change to a larger unit, divide. For decimals of an hour, remember that 0.5 hour is 30 minutes and 0.25 hour is 15 minutes. So 2.5 hours is 2 hours 30 minutes, which is 150 minutes. To find the gap between two times, count up to the next whole hour and then add the rest. For example, from 08:50 to 11:20: 08:50 to 09:00 is 10 minutes, 09:00 to 11:00 is 2 hours, and 11:00 to 11:20 is 20 minutes. That is 2 hours 30 minutes. For dates, count in steps, remembering the length of the month. The 24-hour clock adds 12 to afternoon times, so 18:30 is 6:30pm. To change back, subtract 12. Take care with units in the answer, because 4,500 metres is 4.5 kilometres, not 45.

questions.prompt: How many minutes are there in 2.5 hours?

options.text: 250 minutes
125 minutes
75 minutes
150 minutes

questions.prompt: How many seconds are there in 3 minutes?

options.text: 300 seconds
90 seconds
1,800 seconds
180 seconds

questions.prompt: A journey is 4,500 metres long. How long is it in kilometres?

options.text: 45 km
4.5 km
450 km

questions.prompt: One parcel weighs 750 g and another weighs 250 g. What is their combined weight in kilograms?

options.text: 0.1 kg
10 kg
1 kg

questions.prompt: A training session starts at 08:50 and ends at 11:20. How long does it last?

options.text: 2 hours 70 minutes
2 hours 30 minutes
3 hours 30 minutes
2 hours 10 minutes

questions.hint: 08:50 to 11:00 is 2 hours 10 minutes, plus 20 more minutes makes 2 hours 30.

questions.prompt: A form is received on 5 March and must be dealt with within 10 days of that date. What is the last day for it to be dealt with?

options.text: 14 March
25 March
15 March
16 March

questions.hint: 5 + 10 = 15, counted from the day of receipt.

questions.prompt: A working week is 37.5 hours spread equally over 5 days. How many hours is that a day?

options.text: 5.36 hours
187.5 hours
8.5 hours
7.5 hours

questions.prompt: What is 18:30 on the 12-hour clock?
questions.hint: Subtract 12 from 18 to get 6, and it is the afternoon so pm.

items.title: Numerical reasoning: averages, ratios and simplest form (level 2)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Here you move from reading the definitions to using them on slightly larger sets of numbers. The mean is the total divided by the number of values. If you know the mean and the number of values, you can find the total by multiplying. The median needs the numbers in order from smallest to largest first. The most common mistake is picking the middle of a list that is not sorted. A ratio can be simplified by dividing both parts by the same number, just like a fraction: 12:8 divided by 4 is 3:2. To share an amount in a ratio, add the parts, divide the amount by the total parts to find one part, then multiply. Worked example: share 20 in the ratio 2:3. The parts total 5. One part is 20 ÷ 5 = 4. The smaller share is 2 × 4 = 8 and the larger share is 3 × 4 = 12. If the ratio of staff to managers is 8:1 and there are 4 managers, then each part is 4, so staff number 8 × 4 = 32. Always check that your shares add back up to the starting amount.

questions.prompt: What is the mean of 10, 12, 14 and 16?
What is the median of 4, 9, 2, 7 and 5?
questions.hint: In order the numbers are 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, and the middle one is 5.

questions.prompt: £20 is shared in the ratio 2:3. How much is the larger share?
Which is the ratio 12:8 in its simplest form?
questions.hint: Divide both numbers by 4 to get 3:2.

questions.prompt: The total of six numbers is 90. What is their mean?
In an office the ratio of staff to managers is 8:1. There are 4 managers. How many staff are there?
questions.hint: Staff are 8 parts for every manager, so 4 × 8 = 32.

questions.prompt: The highest score in a test was 95 and the lowest was 62. What is the range?
The mean of three test scores is 80 and two of the scores are 70 and 90. What is the third score?

items.title: Numerical reasoning: tables and charts in words (level 2)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Tables and charts are described in words in some questions, or shown as a small grid in others. Either way, the method is the same. First, work out what the figures represent and the units. Next, find the row and column the question refers to. Then work out what the question wants: a total, a difference, a percentage or a comparison. Worked example: a table shows staff in four offices: Leeds 40, York 25, Hull 30 and Bath 5, making 100 in all. The number in Leeds and Hull together is 40 + 30 = 70. The share of staff in York is 25 out of 100, which is 25%. When the total is 100, the number of people is also the percentage. When it is not 100, divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100. For comparisons across several days or months, write the figures down in a short list first. This helps you find the highest, the lowest and any pair of values with a given total. Check that you used the correct rows and read the units, such as pounds or thousands, before choosing an answer.

questions.prompt: The four offices have 40, 25, 30 and 5 staff, making 100 in total. How many staff work in the two largest offices combined?
questions.hint: The two largest are 40 and 30, so 40 + 30 = 70.

questions.prompt: In a team of 100 staff, 25 work in York. What percentage of the staff work in York?
questions.hint: 25 out of 100 is 25%.

questions.prompt: A call centre answered 85 out of every 100 calls. What percentage of calls went unanswered?
The number of staff in a section fell from 50 to 45. What was the percentage fall?
questions.hint: The fall is 5 out of 50, and 5 ÷ 50 = 0.1, which is 10%.

questions.prompt: Reports filed were 8 on Monday, 12 on Tuesday, 10 on Wednesday, 14 on Thursday and 7 on Friday. Which pair of days together filed exactly 20 reports?

options.text: Wednesday and Thursday
Monday and Tuesday
Tuesday and Wednesday
Thursday and Friday

questions.hint: Monday and Tuesday: 8 + 12 = 20.

questions.prompt: A box holds 120 leaflets. How many leaflets are in 15 boxes?
Team A has 60 cases, Team B has 45 cases and Team C has 30 cases. How many more cases does Team A have than Team C?
Complaints in three months were 18, 22 and 20. What was the mean number a month?

items.title: Numerical reasoning: value for money and everyday comparisons (level 2)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Everyday comparison questions ask which choice is cheaper, how much is left, or how much an amount has changed. To compare two offers fairly, find the price of one item in each: divide the price by the number of items. Then compare the two unit prices. Worked example: a pack of 4 pens costs £2 and a pack of 6 pens costs £2.70. The first costs 50p a pen and the second costs 45p a pen, so the larger pack is better value. A percentage change compares the change with the starting amount: divide the change by the original and multiply by 100. A £3 rise on a £20 fare is 3 ÷ 20 = 0.15, so a 15% rise. To take a percentage off a price, find the amount to take off and subtract it. A 25% reduction on £80 takes off £20 and leaves £60. If you know that a part is a certain percentage of the whole, you can work backwards by dividing: if £200 is 20% of the price, then 1% is £10 and the full price is £1,000. Always check that the answer is realistic. A sale price should be lower than the original, and a bill shared between people should be less than the full bill for each person.

questions.prompt: Pack A has 4 pens for £2. Pack B has 6 pens for £2.70. Which pack is cheaper per pen?

options.text: Pack A, at 50p a pen
Pack B, at 45p a pen
Pack B, at 90p a pen
Pack A, at 25p a pen

questions.hint: £2.70 ÷ 6 = 45p, which is less than £2 ÷ 4 = 50p.

questions.prompt: A train fare rises by £3 from £20. What is the percentage increase?
questions.hint: The rise is 3 ÷ 20 = 0.15, which is 15%.

questions.prompt: A chair costs £80 and is reduced by 25% in a sale. What is the sale price?
A box holds 8 folders. A supplier sends 5 boxes and 12 folders are used. How many folders are left?
A photocopier prints 20 pages a minute. How many pages will it print in 15 minutes?
A deposit of £200 is 20% of the full price. What is the full price?
In a team of 40, five out of every eight people are women. How many men are in the team?
questions.hint: 40 ÷ 8 = 5 per part; 3 parts are men: 3 × 5 = 15.

questions.prompt: A bill of £62.50 is split equally between 5 people. How much does each person pay?

items.title: Verbal reasoning: true, false or cannot say, workplace passages (level 2)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: At this level the passages are a little longer, and the statements test whether you noticed a small word or a missing piece of information. The three verdicts stay the same. True means the passage says it or it follows directly. False means the passage says the opposite. Cannot say means that the passage does not tell you. Method: highlight the key facts, including numbers, names and words such as 'all', 'some', 'only' and 'never'. Then take the statement and look for the exact match. Be careful with statements that combine two ideas, joined by 'and'. Both parts must be supported for the verdict to be True. If one part is clear and the other is not mentioned, it is Cannot say. If one part is contradicted, it is False. Worked example: the passage says 'The team meets weekly on Tuesdays in Room 4.' The statement 'The team meets in Room 4 on Tuesdays' is True. The statement 'The team meets in Room 4 on Tuesdays and Thursdays' is False because the meeting is weekly on Tuesdays. The statement 'The meeting lasts one hour' is Cannot say. Do not bring in your own ideas about what is usual in offices.

questions.prompt: "The team meets weekly on Tuesdays in Room 4. Anyone who cannot attend must send an update to the team leader beforehand." Statement: "Team members who miss a meeting must send an update beforehand." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: those who cannot attend must send an update
False: the update is sent after the meeting
Cannot say: the passage does not name the team leader
Cannot say: the passage does not say how long meetings last

questions.hint: The passage says anyone who cannot attend must send an update beforehand.

questions.prompt: "The finance team has six members. Two of them work part-time and the others work full-time." Statement: "Four members of the finance team work full-time." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: False: only two members work full-time
Cannot say: the passage does not give their hours
Cannot say: the passage does not name the team members
True: six members minus two part-time leaves four

questions.hint: 6 − 2 = 4, so four work full-time.

questions.prompt: "All visitors must wear a badge. Contractors who work on site for more than a week are given a staff pass instead." Statement: "A contractor on site for ten days wears a visitor badge." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: True: all visitors must wear a badge
False: contractors on site for over a week get a staff pass
Cannot say: the passage does not say how long contractors stay
Cannot say: the badge colours are not given

questions.hint: Ten days is more than a week, so a staff pass applies.

questions.prompt: "The canteen sells hot meals between 12 noon and 2pm. Sandwiches and salads are available all day." Statement: "The canteen sells hot meals before noon." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: food is available all day
False: hot meals are served from noon
False: it only sells sandwiches and salads before noon
Cannot say: only the 12 to 2 serving is mentioned

questions.hint: The passage says hot meals are sold 12 to 2, but is silent about earlier.

questions.prompt: "Each employee has 25 days of annual leave plus public holidays. Leave not used by March cannot be carried over." Statement: "Employees can carry unused leave over into the following year." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: False: leave not used by March cannot be carried over
True: employees have 25 days
Cannot say: the passage does not say when the year starts
Cannot say: the number of public holidays is not given

questions.hint: The passage rules out carrying over leave not used.

questions.prompt: "A survey of 200 staff found that 150 use public transport to get to work. The rest travel by car, bike or on foot." Statement: "More than half of the surveyed staff use public transport." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: True: 150 out of 200 is more than half
False: many staff use cars
Cannot say: the passage does not break down the rest
Cannot say: the survey date is not given

questions.hint: 150 is three quarters of 200, which is more than half.

questions.prompt: "The printing budget was cut this year. As a result, staff are asked to print double-sided wherever possible." Statement: "The printing budget was cut because of staff printing habits." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: staff are asked to print less
False: the budget was not cut
False: the cut was made because the printers broke down
Cannot say: the reason for the cut is not given

questions.hint: The passage says what followed the cut, not what caused it.

questions.prompt: "New starters get a laptop on their first day. Laptops are collected from the IT room between 9am and 10am." Statement: "New starters can collect their laptop at 11am." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: laptops are given on the first day
Cannot say: the passage gives only the 9am to 10am window
False: collection is at 9am only
False: laptops are not given on day one

questions.hint: The passage does not say what happens after 10am.

items.title: Verbal reasoning: true, false or cannot say, public information (level 2)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Passages in Civil Service tests often come from the kind of public information that departments publish: leaflets, guidance notes and short news items. The style is plain, but the questions still depend on details. Read the passage once through to get the sense, and a second time to mark the key facts. Think about what kind of statement is being made. If the statement repeats a fact, it is probably True. If it changes one detail, such as a number or a place, it is probably False. If it adds a reason or a prediction that was not given, it is probably Cannot say. Worked example: 'The council will open a new recycling centre in June. It will be open six days a week.' The statement 'The centre will open seven days a week' is False. The statement 'The centre will open on a Monday' is Cannot say, because the passage gives the number of days but not which ones. The council gives June, and a month on its own is not enough to say anything about a season. Keep decisions strictly tied to the words on the page. Aim to spend about a minute on each question in practice.

questions.prompt: "The council has opened a new recycling centre. It is open six days a week and is closed on Mondays." Statement: "The recycling centre is open on Sundays." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: False: recycling centres close at weekends
Cannot say: the passage does not mention Sunday opening times
True: it is open six days and closed only on Mondays
Cannot say: the centre hours are not given

questions.hint: Six days a week with Monday closed means all other days are open, including Sunday.

questions.prompt: "Passport applications from the UK are checked by the Passport Office. Most applications are processed within three weeks." Statement: "All passport applications are processed within three weeks." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: False: the passage says most, not all, are processed in that time
True: applications are checked by the Passport Office
Cannot say: the passage does not name the office
Cannot say: the cost of a passport is not given

questions.hint: 'Most' does not mean 'all'.

questions.prompt: "A new bus route will link the town centre with the hospital. The service will run every 20 minutes from 7am to 7pm." Statement: "A bus will leave the town centre every 20 minutes during the day." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: the passage states the 20-minute frequency
False: the buses will leave every hour
Cannot say: the route is not given
Cannot say: the passage does not say how much tickets cost

questions.hint: The passage says the service runs every 20 minutes between 7am and 7pm.

questions.prompt: "The library service is introducing a new online booking system. Customers can still book by phone or in person." Statement: "Customers will be able to book only online." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: True: a new online system is being introduced
False: phone and in-person booking remain
Cannot say: the passage does not say when it starts
Cannot say: it does not say who built the system

questions.hint: The passage says other ways of booking remain available.

questions.prompt: "Free flu vaccinations are offered at local pharmacies to people aged 65 and over. Appointments are not needed." Statement: "Anyone aged 60 can get a free flu vaccination at a pharmacy." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the passage covers only those aged 65 and over
True: free vaccinations are offered at pharmacies
False: free vaccinations are only offered to people aged 65 and over
False: appointments are needed at pharmacies

questions.hint: A 60-year-old is not covered either way by the passage.

questions.prompt: "Public consultation on the new road scheme closes on 30 June. Responses may be sent by post or online." Statement: "People can send their views on the scheme by post." Using only the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: False: all responses must be made online
True: the passage says responses may be sent by post
Cannot say: the passage does not give an address for posting
Cannot say: the scheme cost is not given

questions.hint: The passage lists post as one of the ways to respond.

questions.prompt: "The museum is free to enter. Special exhibitions cost £8 for adults and £4 for children." Statement: "A child ticket to a special exhibition costs half the adult price." Which option is correct, judged only on the passage?

options.text: False: children pay the full £8
Cannot say: the passage does not name the exhibition
True: £4 is half of £8
Cannot say: the passage does not give the age limit

questions.hint: £4 is exactly half of £8.

questions.prompt: "Heavy rain is forecast for the north of the country on Friday. Road users are advised to check conditions before travelling." Statement: "The rain on Friday will cause flooding." Based only on the passage, which option is correct?

options.text: True: heavy rain causes flooding
False: roads will be clear
False: only the south will be affected
Cannot say: the passage only says heavy rain is forecast

questions.hint: Flooding is not mentioned, so it is not settled by the passage.

items.title: Verbal reasoning: which statement is supported (level 2)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: In this type of question you read a passage and choose which of four statements is supported by it. This is the same skill as true, false or cannot say, but you test four statements at once. The correct statement is the one that is clearly stated or follows directly. Wrong options usually do one of four things: they repeat words from the passage but change the meaning, they add a detail the passage never gave, they overstate with words such as 'always' or 'only', or they mix up cause and effect. Method: read the passage, then take each option in turn and look for evidence. Cross out the ones that clash or go beyond the text. If two seem possible, look again at the exact words. Worked example: 'Applications rose by 10% this year, mostly from people aged 18 to 24.' The statement 'Applications increased this year' is supported. The statement 'Applications from older people fell' is not supported, because nothing is said about older people. The statement 'All applicants were aged 18 to 24' is overstated because the passage says 'mostly'. Choose the option you could point to in the text.

questions.prompt: Applications for the scheme rose by 10% this year, mostly from people aged 18 to 24. Which statement is supported by the passage?

options.text: Applications from older people fell
Applications increased this year
All applicants were aged 18 to 24
The scheme was cheaper to run

questions.hint: The passage says applications rose by 10%.

questions.prompt: The helpline received 3,000 calls in January. In February it received 2,400 calls, because it was closed on three days for staff training. Which statement is supported?

options.text: The helpline took fewer calls in February than in January
The helpline took more calls in February
Staff training took place in January
The helpline closed for a week in February

questions.hint: 3,000 down to 2,400 is a fall in calls.

questions.prompt: A survey found that 70% of customers were satisfied with the online service, compared with 55% for the telephone service. Which statement is supported?

options.text: The telephone service is cheaper
A higher share of customers were satisfied with the online service
Most customers dislike the telephone service
Everyone uses the online service

questions.hint: 70% is higher than 55%.

questions.prompt: The department plans to move three teams to a new building in the spring. It says the move should save money on rent, but it has not yet given an exact figure. Which statement is supported?

options.text: The department has already saved money
The move is expected to take about a year to complete
The department will keep all of its buildings
The department expects the move to reduce rent costs

questions.hint: The passage says the move should save money on rent.

questions.prompt: Last year the call centre answered 90% of calls within one minute. This year the figure was 94%. Which statement is supported?

options.text: The call centre received fewer calls this year
Waiting times were longer this year
Calls were answered within one minute more often this year
The call centre hired more staff

questions.hint: 94% is higher than 90%.

questions.prompt: Three new training courses will start in September: first aid, customer service and fire safety. Places on each course are limited. Which statement is supported?

options.text: Every member of staff will attend all courses
Fire safety training is compulsory
The courses are free
There are courses in first aid, customer service and fire safety

questions.hint: The passage names all three courses.

questions.prompt: The report found that most delays to payments were caused by incomplete forms. A small number were caused by system faults. Which statement is supported?

options.text: Incomplete forms were the main cause of delays
System faults caused most delays
Forms were never incomplete
Delays were never caused by system faults

questions.hint: 'Most' delays were caused by incomplete forms.

questions.prompt: The new office opened in June and now has 120 staff. A further 30 staff are expected to join by December. Which statement is supported?

options.text: The office is expected to have about 150 staff by December
The office opened in December
The office now has 30 staff
The office will close in June

questions.hint: 120 + 30 = 150 expected by December.

items.title: Verbal reasoning: logical conclusions with all, some and none (level 2)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK: Civil Service online tests, practice guidance
items.body: Some verbal questions give you two or three facts using words like all, some and none, and ask what must follow. These questions are logic puzzles in plain words. Draw a small picture if it helps. 'All A are B' means every A is inside B, but B may also have other members. 'Some A are B' means at least one A is B, and it does not tell you about the rest. 'No A are B' means that there is no overlap. Do not turn a statement round. 'All managers have a pass' does not mean 'all pass holders are managers'. Worked example: all the nurses at the clinic wear blue. Hanif wears blue. Is Hanif a nurse? Not necessarily, because other people may wear blue too. But if Hanif does not wear blue, he is not a nurse at the clinic. Another example: 'Some of the staff speak French. Tom is a member of staff.' It is possible that Tom speaks French, but you cannot be sure. Only choose a conclusion that must be true. If the conclusion is merely possible, it is not the answer. Read each option carefully and test it against the facts.

questions.prompt: All the managers on this floor have a pass. Dana is a manager on this floor. Which conclusion must be true?

options.text: Dana is the floor's only manager
Dana has a pass
All pass holders are managers
Dana is a new manager

questions.hint: Every manager on the floor has a pass, and Dana is one.

questions.prompt: All the nurses at the clinic wear blue. Hanif does not wear blue. Which conclusion must be true?

options.text: Hanif works at the clinic
Hanif is not a nurse at the clinic
Hanif is only a visitor to the clinic
Hanif wears green

questions.hint: If all nurses wear blue, a person not in blue cannot be a nurse there.

questions.prompt: Some of the staff speak French. Tom is a member of staff. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Tom speaks French
Tom does not speak French
Tom may or may not speak French
All of the staff here speak French

questions.hint: 'Some' leaves open whether Tom is one of them.

questions.prompt: No one in the finance team works on Fridays. Chen works in the finance team. Which conclusion must be true?

options.text: Chen does not work on Fridays
Chen sometimes works on Fridays
Chen is the team leader
Chen works part-time

questions.hint: No one in the team works Fridays, and Chen is in the team.

questions.prompt: All the reports in the blue folder are urgent. This report is not urgent. Which conclusion must be true?

options.text: This report is probably in the red folder instead
This report is old
This report is not in the blue folder
Most reports are urgent

questions.hint: If all blue-folder reports are urgent, a non-urgent report cannot be in it.

questions.prompt: Some of the volunteers are students. All students get a free lunch. Which statement must be true?

options.text: All volunteers get a free lunch
Some volunteers get a free lunch
Volunteers do not get a free lunch
All students are volunteers

questions.hint: The volunteers who are students get a free lunch.

questions.prompt: Everyone who attends the training will get a certificate. Lucy did not get a certificate. Which conclusion must be true?

options.text: Lucy failed the training
Certificates were not printed
Lucy did not attend the training
Lucy left the training session early

questions.hint: If everyone who attends gets one, someone without one did not attend.

questions.prompt: All the senior staff have a parking space. Some of the part-time staff are senior. Which statement must be true?

options.text: All part-time staff have a parking space
Part-time staff do not have a parking space
Some part-time staff have a parking space
All staff with a space are senior

questions.hint: The senior part-time staff have parking spaces.

items.title: Situational judgement: honesty and accurate records (level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK: The Civil Service Code and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance
items.body: The Civil Service Code asks you to be honest and truthful in everything you do. In an Administrative Officer role, this often means keeping accurate records, reporting what you actually did, and being open when something has gone wrong. Situational judgement questions at this level include small temptations: a deadline that has been missed, a form that is nearly right, or a colleague asking you to cut a corner. The most effective response is usually to be honest quickly, tell the right person and propose a way to put things right. It is less effective to hide the problem, hope it goes away, or blame someone else. Worked example: you have missed a deadline for sending a letter because you were waiting for information. The best response is to tell your manager now, explain the reason, and agree a new date, rather than to send the letter and say nothing about the delay. If you are asked to do something that goes against the rules, explain politely that you cannot and suggest the correct way. Check each option against the question, 'Would I be comfortable telling my manager exactly what I did?'

questions.prompt: You have missed a deadline for sending a letter because you were waiting for information. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell your manager now, explain why and agree a new date
Send it late and say nothing about the delay
Change the date on the letter so that it looks as if it was on time
Ask a colleague to say it was sent on time

questions.hint: Being open about a delay lets your manager manage the impact.

questions.prompt: A colleague asks you to tick a box on a form to say a check has been done, though you did not do it. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tick the box, as you are sure it is fine
Explain that you cannot confirm it and offer to do the check
Tick the box and do the check later
Ask the colleague to tick it themselves

questions.hint: A false record is dishonest; doing the check makes the record true.

questions.prompt: You discover that a spreadsheet you created last week contains a formula error. It has already been shared. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Fix it quietly in your own copy only
Wait to see if anyone notices
Delete the original and say nothing
Correct the error and tell the people who received it

questions.hint: Telling users stops them relying on wrong figures.

questions.prompt: A customer asks whether their application will definitely be approved. You do not know. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say that it probably will be, to reassure them
Say it will be, as they seem eligible
Avoid the question and end the call politely and quickly
Explain that you cannot say and describe the next steps

questions.hint: Do not give promises that you cannot keep.

questions.prompt: You are asked to write a short summary for a decision-maker. The evidence is mixed. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Present the evidence fairly, including points against the preferred option
Include only evidence that supports the preferred option
Leave out the confusing figures
Ask a colleague to choose the figures for you

questions.hint: Advice should be balanced and based on the evidence.

questions.prompt: You find an expense claim you submitted last month included a mistake in your favour. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say nothing, since it is a small amount
Tell your manager or finance team and put it right
Leave it, because they approved it
Claim less next time to balance it

questions.hint: Correcting an overpayment is honest, however small.

questions.prompt: A line manager asks you to record a meeting as taking place on Friday, but it happened on Monday. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Record Friday, as your manager has asked
Explain politely that records must be accurate and suggest the correct date
Record Friday but keep a private note
Leave the date blank without telling them

questions.hint: Records must be accurate even when under pressure.

questions.prompt: You have been given a task and realise halfway through that you misunderstood the instructions. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell the person who set the task and check what is needed
Carry on and hope it is close enough
Start again without telling anyone
Hand it in and say it was what they asked for

questions.hint: Being open about the misunderstanding saves time and builds trust.

items.title: Situational judgement: fairness and treating people equally (level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK: The Civil Service Code and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance
items.body: Impartiality is one of the four Civil Service values. It means acting solely on the merits of a case and serving people of every background equally, regardless of your own views. In practice, an Administrative Officer follows the same process for every customer and every colleague. Situational judgement questions test this with small pressures: someone you know asks for special treatment, a customer is difficult, or a colleague makes a joke that excludes someone. Effective responses apply the rules evenly, explain decisions clearly and challenge or report unfair behaviour calmly. Weak responses favour friends, make assumptions about people, or ignore comments that upset others. Worked example: a neighbour who is applying for a service asks you to put their form to the front of the queue. The best response is to explain that every application is handled in order and offer to tell them how long it should take. Giving them a quicker service would be unfair to others. When you are not sure what the process says, check it or ask a manager. Pick the answer that is fair, polite and clear about the rules.

questions.prompt: A neighbour who has applied for a service asks you to put their form to the front of the queue. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Explain that all applications are handled in order and tell them the expected time
Move it up, as it only takes a moment
Move it up but tell no one
Tell them to ask a friend in another office

questions.hint: Treating everyone the same way is impartial.

questions.prompt: A colleague makes a joke about another person's accent in the break room. The person looks upset. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Laugh along, to avoid conflict
Say nothing, as it was only a joke
Tell the rest of the team about it
Tell your colleague politely that the joke is not appropriate and check on the person

questions.hint: Challenging comments that exclude people helps keep the workplace inclusive.

questions.prompt: You are processing two applications that meet the same criteria. One applicant has been rude to you earlier. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Process both according to the same criteria
Delay the rude applicant's case
Approve the other one first
Ask a colleague to reject the rude applicant's case

questions.hint: Decisions must rest on the criteria, not on personal feelings.

questions.prompt: A customer is wearing unusual clothing and you think they may not be eligible for the service. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Assume they are not eligible and refuse
Ask them to leave
Check their eligibility using the same questions you ask everyone
Ask a colleague what they think of the clothing

questions.hint: Decisions are based on the rules and not on appearance.

questions.prompt: A colleague with a disability asks for a small change to their desk set-up. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell them everyone has to manage with the same desk
Suggest they manage with help from a colleague instead
Ignore the request until they ask again
Help them to make the request through the right route

questions.hint: Supporting reasonable adjustments is fair and follows the rules.

questions.prompt: Your manager asks you to choose between two suppliers for a small order. One is run by a friend of yours. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Choose your friend, as they are reliable
Choose the other supplier to avoid any problems
Tell your manager about the friendship and ask for another person to decide
Choose quietly without saying anything

questions.hint: Declaring a conflict of interest keeps the decision fair.

questions.prompt: A customer asks you to explain why they were refused a service, and you think the decision was harsh. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say that you agree it was harsh
Say the decision was made by someone else
Explain the rules that were applied and how they can appeal
Tell them the rules do not apply to them

questions.hint: Explaining the rules and the appeal route is honest and fair.

questions.prompt: A new colleague from a different country asks a question that you think is obvious. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say they should know that already
Answer politely and clearly
Tell others how basic the question was
Suggest they look it up themselves

questions.hint: Everyone should be treated with courtesy and respect.

items.title: Situational judgement: priorities and deadlines (level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK: The Civil Service Code and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance
items.body: Administrative work is full of competing tasks. Situational judgement questions often ask what you should do first when two or more things need attention. The principles are simple. Work out what is urgent, which means it has to be done soon, and what is important, which means it matters most for the service or for people's safety. Anything that affects safety or a legal deadline comes first. Then consider how many people are affected and how long the task will take. If you cannot do everything, tell your manager early and agree what to do, rather than let something slip. It also helps to write a to-do list and update it. Worked example: your manager asks for a report by midday, a colleague asks you to check a form that is due next week, and a customer rings with a question. The most effective approach is to tell your colleague you will help after the report, take the customer's details and ring them back later, and focus on the report. If you do not know what is more urgent, ask. Avoid answers that leave tasks unfinished without telling anyone.

questions.prompt: Your manager needs a report by midday. A colleague asks for help with a form due next week. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Help your colleague first, because they asked first
Tell your colleague you cannot ever help
Finish the report first and offer to help your colleague afterwards
Do both at the same time without a plan

questions.hint: The report has the earlier deadline, so it comes first.

questions.prompt: You have three tasks and are not sure which your manager wants first. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Pick the easiest task first
Do them in the order you received them
Wait for your manager to ask
Ask your manager which is the priority

questions.hint: Asking removes uncertainty and avoids wasted effort.

questions.prompt: You are halfway through filing documents when a visitor arrives at reception and there is nobody else free. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Finish all the filing first
Wave to the visitor from your desk
Ask the visitor to come back later
Stop and greet the visitor, then go back to the filing

questions.hint: A waiting visitor needs a prompt response and filing can wait a few minutes.

questions.prompt: You realise you will not finish a task by the end of the day because of an unexpected request. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Stay silent and hope for more time
Rush the task and risk mistakes
Tell your manager and agree a new deadline
Pass it to a colleague without telling them

questions.hint: Telling the manager early allows them to adjust plans.

questions.prompt: A colleague asks you to look at an urgent customer letter while you are in the middle of a task. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Refuse because you are busy
Find out how urgent it is and fit it in if it is more important
Do it immediately and forget your own task
Ask them to wait until next week

questions.hint: Checking urgency helps you decide properly.

questions.prompt: You find out that a form with a legal deadline has not been sent. The deadline is today. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Wait until the afternoon to see if it is needed
Send it tomorrow and apologise
Tell your manager straight away and send it as soon as possible
Ask a colleague to explain it

questions.hint: A legal deadline today is the top priority.

questions.prompt: You are asked to arrange a meeting for eight people with different diaries. What is the most effective first step?

options.text: Check everyone's availability and suggest a few times
Pick a time and tell everyone to attend
Book a room and send no invitation
Ask only the most senior person

questions.hint: Checking availability first avoids rearranging later.

questions.prompt: At the start of the week you receive many emails. What is the most effective way to deal with them?

options.text: Delete older emails
Read them, sort them by urgency and reply to the urgent ones first
Reply to every email in the order they arrived
Leave them until Friday

questions.hint: Sorting by urgency means important matters are handled promptly.

items.title: Situational judgement: working with information and data (level 2)
items.source: GOV.UK: The Civil Service Code and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance
items.body: Administrative staff handle information about real people, such as names, addresses, bank details and health information. The Civil Service takes data protection seriously, and situational judgement questions test whether you handle it carefully. The basic rules are to share information only with people who need it for their work, to check who you are talking to before you share anything, to keep documents out of sight, and to report any loss or mistake straight away. Never discuss customers' details in public places or on social media. Emails with personal details should be sent only to the right addresses. Worked example: you realise you sent an email containing a customer's details to the wrong person. The most effective response is to tell your manager or the data protection contact immediately, so that the department can contain the problem. It is not effective to ask the person to delete it and say nothing more. Being quick matters, because a fast report lets the department limit any harm and meet its legal duties. Think about what could go wrong for the customer and choose the response that protects them.

questions.prompt: You realise you emailed a customer's details to the wrong person. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask the person to delete it and say nothing more
Tell your manager or the data protection contact straight away
Hope that they ignore it
Send a second email with different details

questions.hint: A prompt report lets the department limit any harm.

questions.prompt: A caller says they are a customer's relative and asks for details of the customer's claim. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Explain that you cannot share details without the customer's permission
Share the details, as they are family
Share the details if they know the address
Share only the amount

questions.hint: Personal data can only be shared with the right person or with consent.

questions.prompt: You are on a train and want to finish a report that contains personal details. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Work on it anyway, but sit by the window
Read it aloud to check it
Take photos of the screen to work on later
Wait until you are somewhere private rather than work on it in public

questions.hint: Private information should not be exposed in public places.

questions.prompt: A friend asks on social media what kind of cases your office handles most. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Share a few examples without names
Describe a recent case briefly
Do not discuss details of your work and reply with general information only
Tell them to ask your manager

questions.hint: Work details should not be shared on social media.

questions.prompt: You find a paper with customer details on the printer. Nobody is nearby. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Leave it where it is
Put it in the recycling bin
Take it, keep it secure and hand it to the owner or your manager
Read it to see who it belongs to

questions.hint: Paper with personal data should be kept secure and returned.

questions.prompt: You are asked to send a spreadsheet of customer data to a colleague in another team. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Send it to their personal email
Send it to the whole team
Print it and leave it on their desk
Check they need it, then send it by a secure method

questions.hint: Only share data with those who need it, using secure means.

questions.prompt: You leave your desk for a meeting. Your screen shows a customer's record. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Lock your screen before you leave
Turn the monitor away from the aisle
Leave it open, since you will not be long
Ask a colleague to watch your desk

questions.hint: Locking the screen prevents others from viewing the record.

questions.prompt: You receive an email asking you to click a link to update your password urgently. You do not recognise the sender. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Do not click and report it as suspicious
Click the link, as it might be genuine
Reply to the sender to ask if the email is genuine
Forward it to all your colleagues

questions.hint: Suspicious emails should be reported and not opened.
